transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-05
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes (recording ended at ~15:58)
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Diego Marquez (Redwood SE), Rajiv Patel (Stellarmap Head of ML), Maya Chen (CTO), Oliver Grant (Infra)

Summary:
Quick intro to Stellarmap's planned production timeline and constraints, deep dive on per-token unit economics and batch/cache levers, specific KV-cache heavy traffic concerns for short-turnaround prompts, and pilot/pricing ask. Action items and benchmarking next steps agreed.

Topics covered:
- Current stack and where inference will run (hosted vs dedicated vs private VPC)
- Per-token economics, batching, caching and quantization tradeoffs
- SLA & throughput expectations and fallback policies
- Pilot scope and security/compliance ask (SOC2, SSO, KMS)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we should be starting, uh, in a couple minutes, appreciate you blocking time. Quick round of intros?
[00:10] Rajiv Patel: Rajiv here, head of machine learning at Stellarmap, we run a map tagging product, low-latency NER plus prompt ensembling, we want under 140 ms p95 ideally.
[00:18] Maya Chen: Maya, CTO, focused on cost and infra ops, y'know, we're watching spend closely this quarter.
[00:22] Oliver Grant: Oliver, infra lead, I own network, VPC peering and on-prem connectors.
[00:26] Diego Marquez: Diego from Redwood, platform SE, I'll cover benchmarks and the KV-cache stuff.
[00:30] Lena Park: Great. So the agenda is to map your latency/cost requirements and how Redwood's hosted/dedicated/private options fit. We'll focus on token-level economics and batching/cache levers you can pull.

[03:05] Rajiv: To kick off — we're running a mixture of short prompts ~20-80 tokens, but we also do some long prompt concat for multi-step ensembling. Most traffic is high QPS spikes, like short bursts when external customers run scans.
[03:32] Maya: And for budget, finance gave us a hard cap — $60k/mo for inference in year-one for production. We may do a pilot at smaller scale, but we need to model the run rate.

[04:40] Diego: That's useful. For short prompts, batching helps but only up to a point — continuous batching introduces latency. We usually recommend prefix KV caching + small batch windows to hit cost targets without blowing p95. For your 140 ms p95 target, we need to look at end-to-end stack and network egress.

[05:58] Oliver: We're sensitive about data residency and audit logs — SOC2 is a must, and we'll need SAML/SSO + KMS integration if we go private. Does Redwood offer a private deployment package?
[06:20] Lena: Yes, we do Redwood Private with VPC and on-prem options, integrates with customer KMS/HSM and provides audit logs. For most customers with your constraints, they start hosted to iterate then migrate to Dedicated or Private for isolation and consistent performance.

[07:44] Rajiv: Show me the math — per-token pricing differences between hosted and dedicated — also, how batching/caching changes that math.
[08:03] Lena: Sure. Hosted per-token is simple to start; dedicated is a committed capacity model with lower unit cost but an infra commit. Key levers: 1) batch size/distribution 2) KV/prefix cache hit rate 3) model choice and quantization.

[09:21] Diego: Example: if you have 20M tokens per month at median prompt length 40, with no caching and small batches you might hit X cost on hosted. With KV cache that hits 40% of tokens we reduce token generation by that hit amount — effectively lowering per-response token cost. Also continuous batching can reduce per-token GPU overhead, but it adds latency — some customers use micro-batching windows of 5-15 ms.

[10:15] Maya: What's the real-life delta? Numbers please, rough order of magnitude.
[10:20] Diego: Back-of-envelope: Hosted baseline maybe $0.0007 per token for a given model family, with batching and cache you might get to $0.00028 equivalent per generated token effective cost, or lower if you commit to Dedicated and choose quantized variants. Those numbers vary a lot by model size and sequence length.

[11:40] Rajiv: Right, but we need an internal forecast to map to the $60k cap. If batching and cache give us 50% reduction, we can afford higher QPS.

[12:05] Diego: We'll share a spreadsheet that models per-token burn across hosted/dedicated/private with inputs: average prompt length, cache hit rate, target p95 latency, and commit term. That's the pilot pricing doc Lena will send.

[14:50] Oliver: About the KV cache — our traffic is KV-heavy because many prompts reuse prefixes for map tiles; how does Redwood's prefix/KV cache work operationally? Where is the cache stored?
[15:16] Diego: We support both in-memory KV caching at the runtime layer and optional external cache (Redis) for cross-instance persistence. For hosted we provide managed prefix caching that lives in the serving layer; for Dedicated or Private you can surface your own Redis for stronger locality.
[16:02] Rajiv: Is there a hit for cache lookup latency? If we go to external Redis across AZs we might add 5-10 ms.
[16:12] Diego: Yes, network-bound cache lookups can add latency; our evals show local in-runtime KV hits are sub-ms, external redis calls depend on topology. For p95 budgets you'll want cache close to serving nodes or use Dedicated to keep everything co-located.

[18:00] Maya: If we choose Dedicated, what are the minimum commit terms and refund/scale policies? We don't want to be stuck with trucks of GPUs.
[18:22] Lena: Typical committed terms are monthly or annual; there are burst and auto-scale policies so you don't need to over-provision for spikes. We can propose a 3-month pilot commit with credit towards an annual contract if you convert.

[19:10] Rajiv: What about quantization? Could we quantize models safely without big regressions? We care about NER quality.
[19:26] Diego: Quantization to int8 or 4-bit can drastically reduce memory and improve throughput, but accuracy impact depends on model and eval prompts. Redwood Optimize recommends quantization profiles per workload; we can run an eval on your prompt set to measure regression risk.

[21:05] Oliver: On security, can hosted meet our audit needs? Or do we need Private from day one?
[21:18] Lena: Hosted has SOC2 + standard logging; Private gives you more control (KMS/HSM integrated, VPC peering, no shared tenancy). For regulated customers we usually start with Private evals, but if your compliance team is okay with SOC2 hosted plus contractual terms, many customers iterate faster on hosted.

[23:00] Rajiv: Performance question — high variance traffic means some 99p latency spikes. How does Redwood handle graceful degradation?
[23:14] Diego: We support smart routing and automatic fallbacks to smaller/lighter model variants and cross-region fallback. Also token-slicing and request prioritization lets you keep high-priority traffic hot. These reduce downtime or severe latency spikes at expense of quality or cost.

[25:40] Maya: For our forecast, we need a sensitivity table: best/worst/midcase for cache hit rates (20/50/80%), batch windows (5/20/50 ms), and commit types. Can you produce that?
[25:58] Lena: Yes — that's part of the pricing workbook. We'll fill scenarios and highlight what stays within $60k/mo.

[28:10] Rajiv: Also curious about per-request overhead for short prompts — tokenization, request parse, network — how much of the 140 ms p95 is out of our control?
[28:28] Diego: Tokenization is small but non-zero — 3-8 ms typically. Network egress and client-side retry strategies can add variance. At p95, the server-side model generation plus fetch time is usually the dominant component. We'll run a microbenchmark to break that down.

[31:02] Oliver: Any gotchas re: VPC peering and egress costs?
[31:18] Lena: VPC peering is supported; egress billing depends on cloud region and whether data crosses regions. In Private deployments, you can keep everything in-region to minimize egress. We'll include network cost lines in the workbook.

[33:40] Rajiv: Competitor question — why Redwood vs Vertex AI or Anthropic if they have easy endpoints?
[33:56] Lena: Two things: production economics focus (granular levers for batching, caching, quantization) and unified ops across hosted/dedicated/private. Many customers start with another provider then realize they need more control over unit economics at scale.

[36:00] Maya: Ok so what's a realistic pilot? We don't want long procurement.
[36:12] Lena: Proposed pilot: 6 weeks, basic security review, one week of actual benchmarks with your prompt set, then 4 weeks of live traffic on a capacity slice (dedicated or hosted) to observe unit econ. We'll price a small reserved pool and measure.

[37:50] Rajiv: Can we run a dark-launch where 10% of traffic goes to Redwood to compare latencies and token burn?
[38:02] Diego: Yep, dark-launch is a standard approach; we can instrument costs and metrics at token granularity so you can do apples-to-apples.

[40:30] Oliver: On observability — do you expose token-level cost per route and trace logs?
[40:42] Diego: Yes, Redwood Console provides token-level cost, per-route latency histograms, and traces; we emit structured logs and can ship to your SIEM or S3.

[42:15] Rajiv: What do you need from us to size the pilot?
[42:24] Lena: Short list: sample prompt set (representative of short and long flows), QPS distribution, desired p95 targets, and network topology. Rajiv said they'd provide that.

[44:10] Maya: Also, include the SLA targets we can expect for Dedicated in writing.
[44:18] Lena: We'll include SLA and pilot conversion credit language.

[46:55] Diego: Small note on cache hit measurement — we will instrument hit/miss metrics; we recommend you run a short warm-up to populate prefix cache before measuring steady-state savings. Warm-up scripts are in the benchmark plan I'll send.

[48:30] Rajiv: Anything about embeddings? We use embeddings for reranking; cost there scales differently.
[48:42] Diego: Embeddings are billed differently; you can run embeddings on dedicated pools with different quantization and batching rules. We'll add an embeddings sheet in the workbook.

[50:05] Maya: Timeline — procurement and security approval will take 3-4 weeks, pilot after that. Is that realistic?
[50:18] Lena: Yes — with SOC2 docs and a short security Q&A, 3-4 weeks is normal. If you want Private from day one it'll add lead time for VPC setup but still manageable.

[52:00] Rajiv: Ok let's recap next steps.
[52:10] Lena: Recap: 1) We'll send pilot pricing workbook + scenarios 2) Diego will send benchmark plan + warm-up script 3) Stellarmap will provide prompt set, QPS distribution, and latency targets 4) Schedule a 2-hour benchmark window for the week of Apr 13.
[52:35] Maya: Agree. Please include SOC2 PDFs and network diagram.
[52:40] Oliver: I'll be the point on infra and will take the benchmark coordination.

[54:00] Rajiv: Quick question — what's the typical cache hit rate you see for map-tile style reuse?
[54:10] Diego: Customers with high prefix reuse see 40-70% hit rates for certain flows; it depends on how much prompt variation you have. We'll baseline that in the benchmark.

[55:15] Lena: Great, we'll follow up via email with the docs and calendar invites. Thanks everyone.
[55:28] Meeting ended.

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-hears around acronyms (KMS/HSM sometimes transcribed as K-M-S H-S-M), and KV cache was sometimes written as "K V cash" by auto-transcribe. Some short crosstalk omitted.
